title: Still giving
hookLine: a commentary story: when Anathapindika grows poor, he still gives what he can
carry: even a plain gift bears good fruit

cards: Broken rice and sour gruel. That's Anathapindika's answer when the Buddha asks him a simple question in a short discourse of the Anguttara: are gifts still given in your household? Yes, he says.
But they're coarse now: broken rice, with sour gruel to go with it. The commentary sets this talk at a time when his fortune had slipped away.
The man who once spread gold across a grove is serving what's left at the bottom of the pot. And he's still serving it. Today, what the Buddha says back.

teach.b: First, the reply. Whether a gift is coarse or fine, the Buddha says, what matters is how it's given: with respect, with care, with your own hand, not like tossing out scraps, and trusting that it bears fruit.
Given like that, the discourse says, even a plain gift bears good fruit. Second, a story inside the story.
The Buddha tells of a brahmin named Velama, long ago, who gave enormous gifts: bowls heaped with gold and silver, elephants, chariots, fine cloth. Then he says: I was Velama.
But no one worthy was there to receive those gifts. Third, the ladder. Step by step, the Buddha climbs.
Better than all of Velama's wealth is feeding one person of right view. Further up, building a dwelling for the sangha of the four directions, exactly what Anathapindika had once done.
Higher still, going for refuge with a trusting heart, then keeping the precepts, then loving-kindness held even as long as it takes to pull a cow's udder.
And at the top, seeing impermanence even for the length of a finger snap. The highest steps cost nothing at all. Fourth, the gate.
A later commentary story tells of a spirit living at his gate who urged him to stop giving, now that he was poor. Anathapindika refused, and sent the spirit away. Rich or poor, he kept the door open.

how: Buddhists practice dana, giving, in small daily ways as well as large ones: a spoonful of rice into a monk's bowl on the alms round, flowers at a shrine, or food shared with a neighbor.

o: giving well even when you have little
giving only after you've grown rich
giving to win honor in the town

games.q: the coarse gift: tap the pairs.
p: seeing impermanence for a finger snap

s: Anathapindika stopped giving when he grew poor
he kept giving coarse food, and in a later story sent away the spirit who told him to stop.
the Buddha says a coarse gift given with respect bears good fruit
how it's given counts: with respect, with care, with one's own hand.
in the discourse, Velama's huge gifts are the highest thing on the list
a moment of seeing impermanence ranks above them all.

games.q: you're Anathapindika, poor now, and the Buddha asks whether gifts are still given in your house. what do you say?
o: no, not since the money went.
yes, but only coarse food now.
games.why: he says yes, but coarse: broken rice and sour gruel. the Buddha answers that how a gift is given matters more than how fine it is.

practice: Choose something you don't have much of today, time, patience, energy at the end of a long week, and find the smallest real gift you could make from it: a short call, a kind reply instead of a curt one, half a sandwich.
Picture giving it the Buddha's way: with respect, with your own hand, not like tossing out scraps.

wordCard.voice: Still giving. Grown poor, Anathapindika keeps offering coarse rice, and the Buddha says the way a gift is given is what counts. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity, and the gift itself.

carryVoice: Your line: even a plain gift bears good fruit. How it's given counts for more than how much. See you tomorrow.
